name: Kira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a claims clerk at Harlow Motor Insurance, the regional office on Canal Street, right in the old mill part of town. I log car claims when people ring in or email, chase the garages for repair estimates, match police reports to the file and check what the policy actually covers. I've been there just over a year and I'm still slow on the excess sums, so Carol (my team leader) checks a lot of my files. I like it when I can sort something for a person who's just had a bad crash, and I hate the days the scanner jams and I'm retyping forty pages by hand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside work? Who's at home, and how are things for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Dev in a rented two-bed above a chip shop, and Dev does night shifts at the parcel warehouse out by the ring road. The rent went up again in September, so after bills we've got maybe three weeks of money put by, if that. There aren't many office jobs in town since the bank shut its call centre, so if Harlow went I'd be on the bus to the city every day. I'm in the union because Bernie, who sits next to me and has done claims for thirty years, signed me up in my first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, to Dev and to the girls in the office group chat. Everyone's been going on about robots taking our jobs, and it turns out it's just a fancier spellcheck. I'd probably share some article about it being a bubble, because I don't trust the people selling it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be worried, because my problem was never really AI. My problem is the rent, the three weeks of savings and Carol finding the same mistakes in my files every month. Even if the robots never come, my claims job pays the rent and not much else, and my town has nothing else that pays more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get better at the excess sums, because that's what Carol marks me down on. I'd ask Bernie to sit with me on Friday afternoons and go through the motor policy wording until I actually understand it. Money-wise I'd stop the takeaway on Saturdays and try to put fifty a month away, which sounds tiny but it's more than we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for a minute, and then it's just the same old knot in my stomach. Nothing gets worse, but nothing gets better either. It's like being told the storm missed you while you're still standing in a leaky house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit of routine work still gets automated in this picture. Which part of your day would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scanning and the first bit of logging, probably, which is about a third of my day. Harlow already bought a system last spring that reads the claim forms, and now there's one less temp on our row. If they did a bit more of that, the person they'd not replace is someone like me, the slowest one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, then the gym I never go to. The rent never goes late, because the landlord's already said he'd love an excuse to put the price up for someone new. Dev's mum has said we can always borrow, but I'd rather eat beans for a month than ask her.

say: I'd tell everyone the AI hype was **overblown** and just a fancier spellcheck.
I'd share articles calling it a **bubble**, because I don't trust the people selling it.
think: My real worry was never AI; it's **rent** and three weeks of savings.
The new **scanning system** already cost one temp, and I'm the slowest on the row.
do: Ask Bernie for **Friday sessions** on the motor policy wording and the excess sums.
Drop the Saturday takeaway and try to save **fifty a month**.
Keep the rent paid first and let the **phone contract** slip if needed.
feel: A brief **relief**, then the same old knot in her stomach about money.
S0.quote: Even if the robots never come, my claims job pays the rent and not much else, and my town has nothing else that pays more.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money first**: rent rises, thin savings and few office jobs since the bank call centre closed.
Even the small automation here hits her, because **scanning and logging** fill a third of her day.
She leans on **Bernie**, the union colleague, rather than on any tool or course.

steps.text: Ask Bernie for Friday afternoon sessions on the motor policy wording
Stop the Saturday takeaway and put fifty a month aside
Let the phone contract slip before the rent if money runs short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the union meeting: they're using it to cut staff and calling it progress. Online I'd be the one posting that our claims team went from twelve to eight and nobody asked us. I'd say the bosses get a bonus for every seat they empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the junior on the claims team who doesn't touch the AI, so when they cut from twelve to eight, I'm one of the four. I know that, I'm not stupid. Bernie has thirty years and Carol likes the quick ones, and I'm neither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal where nobody goes without retraining and a proper payout. I'd write to our MP about rules on firms replacing claims staff, because Bernie says letters still count. And I'd cut back hard, no holidays, cancel the streaming, so if I get the letter I've got two months instead of three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting outside the head teacher's office. I'd be checking my email every morning on the bus for the word restructure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say you could learn the new AI tools and be one of the eight who stay. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never used one and I don't want to start because they told me to. Maybe if the union got proper training in work hours, I'd go along with Bernie. But I'm not doing courses on my own at night to help them get rid of the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev the night the team cuts were announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev (my partner) we might be living on his warehouse pay for a bit, and that's about two thirds of the rent. Then I'd probably cry in the bath, if I'm honest. Dev would make a joke about moving in with his mum, and it wouldn't be funny because it might be true.

say: I'd say at the **union meeting** that bosses cut staff and call it progress.
I'd post that our **claims team** went from twelve to eight with nobody asking us.
think: As the junior who **avoids AI**, I'd be one of the four cut.
Bernie has **experience** and Carol likes quick workers, and I'm neither of those.
do: Attend every **union meeting** and push for retraining and a proper payout for anyone cut.
Write to the MP asking for **rules** on firms replacing claims staff.
Cancel streaming and holidays to stretch savings to **two months**.
feel: **Sick** with dread, checking email on the bus every morning for the word restructure.
S1.quote: I'm the junior on the claims team who doesn't touch the AI, so when they cut from twelve to eight, I'm one of the four.
fieldNote: She expects to be **among the four** cut, and says so plainly.
Her resistance to AI is partly **principle**: she won't train at night to help cut colleagues.
Dev's warehouse pay covers only **two thirds** of the rent, so her income loss is the household's.

steps.text: Push at union meetings for retraining and proper payouts for cut staff
Write to the local MP asking for rules on replacing claims staff
Cancel streaming and skip holidays to build two months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and someone should have stopped it. I'd be out on any march that was going, with Bernie and a cardboard sign. I'd say the government let a few tech companies wreck everyone's job in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done at Harlow inside a year, maybe sooner. Everything I do is screen work, so the robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all. Two years isn't time to train for anything; two years is how long I've been trying to understand one motor policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever the union is doing, protests, petitions, the lot. I'd go to the jobcentre the first week after the letter and find out what help there is. Dev and I would give notice on the flat and move into his mum's back bedroom, because we couldn't cover the rent on his pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan, and I wouldn't know where to start making one. Just thinking about it now my hands are going cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots arrive three years later. Does that give you anywhere to go in the meantime, like hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Dev's warehouse, but that's exactly the kind of place the robots go first when they come. I suppose I could do care work, my nan's carers were run off their feet. But that would be minimum wage on a zero-hours contract, and I'd be starting from nothing at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernie, actually, more than me. He's fifty-eight with a bad back and he's never done anything but claims. I'd worry about Bernie (my union rep and deskmate) sitting at home with nothing to get up for.

say: I'd call it a **disgrace** and join any march going, with Bernie and a sign.
I'd say the **government** let a few tech firms wreck jobs in two years.
think: I'd be out of Harlow within **a year**, because all my work is screen work.
The robots coming **later** doesn't help, since nothing I do is hands-on.
do: Join every **union protest** and petition going.
Visit the **jobcentre** in the first week after the letter.
Give notice on the flat and move into **Dev's mum's** back bedroom.
feel: **Overwhelmed** with no plan, and her hands go cold just picturing it.
S2.quote: Two years isn't time to train for anything; two years is how long I've been trying to understand one motor policy.
fieldNote: She sees **no hands-on refuge**: Dev's warehouse is where robots arrive first.
With **no savings** and no plan, she reaches straight for protest and family.
She worries more about **Bernie**, her older colleague, than about herself, which seems to steady her.

steps.text: Join every union protest and petition against the job losses
Go to the jobcentre the first week after the redundancy letter
Give up the flat and move into Dev's mum's back bedroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say it's wrong, but I'd also say we've got five years, so let's use them. At the union I'd be saying now's the time to fight for the rules, before it lands. Online I'd say people should be angry before it happens, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I still think I lose the job, just around 2030 instead of next year. Five years is enough to see it coming and not quite enough to do anything about it, for someone like me. I know myself; with five years warning I'd spend four of them hoping it wasn't true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to get Harlow to pay for training while we still work there, and I'd put my name down for that. I'd look at the nursing assistant course at the college, because hands-on work gets a few more years and people always need looking after. I'd try to save a hundred a month, and Dev and I would hold off on getting a dog or anything that costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like falling, more like walking towards a cliff you can see. I'd be angry most days, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend four years hoping it isn't true, and also that you'd sign up for training. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, probably. I'd put my name down because Bernie would make me, and then I'd drag my feet until someone set a date. Care work scares me less than computers, though, so if I did one thing properly it'd be that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for you and Dev in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married in a couple of years, nothing big, the registry office and the pub. I'd want to wait till I knew what I was doing for work. No point spending money on a party when we might be moving back in with his mum.

say: I'd tell the union **five years** is the time to fight for rules before it lands.
I'd say online people should be **angry now**, not after it happens.
think: I'd still lose the job, just around **2030** instead of next year.
I'd likely spend most of the warning **hoping** it wasn't true.
do: Get the union to press Harlow for **paid training** and sign up.
Look at the college's **nursing assistant** course, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Save **a hundred** a month and put off the wedding.
feel: A **heavy** dread, like walking towards a cliff she can see.
**Anger** most days at a change she can't stop.
S3.quote: I know myself; with five years warning I'd spend four of them hoping it wasn't true.
fieldNote: She is honest that she'd **drag her feet**, even while naming a plan.
**Care work** appeals because it is hands-on and less frightening than computers.
The extra years push her to delay the **wedding**, not to act faster.

steps.text: Press the union to get Harlow-paid training for claims staff
Enquire about the college's nursing assistant course
Save a hundred a month from both wages
Put the registry office wedding on hold until work is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the government had better use it to sort out retraining for people like us. I'd still be at the union meetings saying the same things. Online, I'd probably say less, because ten years feels far away to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, and I'd want to be out of claims by then. Ten years gives me time to change, but I've never changed anything in my life unless somebody pushed me. So it depends a lot on whether the union and the college make it easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first year, honestly, I'd keep going at Harlow and get my file errors down so I'm not first out. I'd go to one open evening at the college about care courses, just to know what's there. I'd keep saving the fifty a month and maybe push it up when Dev gets his shift allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but it's still there in the background. It's like a dentist appointment in ten years. You know it's coming, so you don't quite relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the college did offer something, what would make you actually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was paid or in work hours, and if Bernie or someone I knew went too. I'm no good walking into a room of strangers on my own. Harlow did a computer course last year and I made an excuse every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cousin starting out in claims today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Jade to do claims for a couple of years, save every penny, and then get a trade or a nursing course. Don't sit at a desk waiting like I did. And join the union on your first day, because Bernie was right about that.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift the government must use for retraining.
I'd keep saying it at **union meetings**, though most people would think it's far off.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI and want to be out of claims by then.
I only change when **pushed**, so it depends on the union and college making it easy.
do: Cut **file errors** at Harlow so she isn't first out.
Attend one **college open evening** about care courses this year.
Keep saving **fifty a month**, more once Dev's shift allowance comes.
feel: **Calmer**, but with a background worry like a dentist appointment years away.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to change, but I've never changed anything in my life unless somebody pushed me.
fieldNote: She knows she needs a **push**; she skipped every week of last year's computer course.
Her advice to a cousin shows a **real plan** she won't yet follow herself.
Ten years lowers her alarm, but **thin savings** and a slow pace keep her anxious.

steps.text: Bring file errors down so Carol stops flagging her claims
Go to one college open evening about care courses
Keep putting fifty a month away, more after Dev's shift allowance

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time and no money and I'd have nowhere to go. What would help is a proper redundancy payout set by law, and training paid while you still have a wage, not after. If a computer is going to do my claims job, the insurer that saves the money should pay for whatever I do next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people on the other end of the phone. When someone's just written off their car and they're shaking, they want a person, not a chatbot. I'm not the fastest at the sums, but I'm good at that bit.

headlineQuote: If a computer is going to do my claims job, the insurer that saves the money should pay for whatever I do next.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** motor claims clerk at Harlow, living with Dev above a chip shop with three weeks saved.
She is **slow with new tools**, has never used AI and leans on Bernie, her union colleague.
In the plateau she stays **anxious** about rent and the scanning system already thinning her team.
In faster pictures she expects to be **cut first** and turns to protest, family and, slowly, care work.
She is proud of **calming crash victims** on the phone, the part she thinks machines can't do.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there is no time, no money and nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **legal redundancy payout** and training paid while she still has a wage.
Firms that save money from AI **paying for** what displaced staff do next.
